title: Simulated: 100-200 item benchmarks rarely resolve a 5-point gap
summary: Monte Carlo simulation, binary-scored items at about 70% accuracy, item-level correlation between arms about 0.25-0.64: a paired bootstrap 95% CI detects a true 5-point gap in only 13-19% of 100-item comparisons and 20-34% of 200-item ones; at 500 items detection rises to 51-76%. At that gap the median CI half-width is 8.0-10.5 pp at n=100, 5.8-7.8 pp at n=200 and 3.6-4.8 pp at n=500 (pooled over gaps 0-10: 7.5-11.0, 5.3-7.8, 3.4-4.9).

statement.text: In a Monte Carlo simulation of two systems scored pass/fail on the same items at about 70% baseline accuracy (item-level correlation between the arms about 0.25-0.64), a paired bootstrap 95% CI on the accuracy difference excludes zero for a true 5-point gap in only 13-19% (100 items), 20-34% (200) and 51-76% (500) of comparisons; at that gap its median half-width is 8.0-10.5 points at 100 items, 5.8-7.8 at 200 and 3.6-4.8 at 500 (7.5-11.0, 5.3-7.8 and 3.4-4.9 pooled over true gaps of 0-10 points); with no true gap it excludes zero in 3.5-5.2% of comparisons.
qualifiers: Ranges span the two simulated dependence settings: a shared-difficulty mixing probability rho of 0.5 and 0.8, which induce an item-level correlation between the arms' correctness of about 0.25 and 0.64 (rho squared); higher item-level correlation narrows the CI.
400 simulated comparisons per cell and 1000 bootstrap resamples: one standard error of a detection rate is about 1-2.5 points (a 95% interval about +/-2-5 points).
doesNotClaim: That any particular real benchmark has these item correlations.
Anything about continuous or partial-credit metrics, or about averaging several seeds per item.
That a non-significant difference proves the systems are equal.
Anything about item-level correlations outside about 0.25-0.64, or about bootstrap intervals other than the percentile interval used here.

evidence.title: Simulation script (stdlib Python, fixed seed)
evidence.description: Regenerates results.csv exactly: python3 paired_bootstrap_sim.py > results.csv. Uses only the Python standard library.
evidence.derivation: Per item, each arm independently reuses a shared difficulty draw with probability rho (the mixing probability), otherwise takes its own draw; arm B's threshold is raised by the true gap. Both arms share the draw with probability rho squared, so the item-level correlation of correctness is about rho squared (0.25 / 0.64), not rho.

assessor.name: AI reviewer: claude-code (its own one-shot model)

assessments.scope: Monte Carlo simulation (stdlib Python, seed 20261014) of two systems with binary per-item correctness. Baseline accuracy is 70% for arm A, and arm B's threshold is raised by the true gap. Item counts are 100, 200 and 500. True gaps are 0, 3, 5 and 10 points. The shared-difficulty mixing probability rho is 0.5 or 0.8, giving an item-level correlation of about 0.25 or 0.64 (rho squared). Each cell has 400 comparisons and 1000 bootstrap resamples. The analysis is a percentile paired bootstrap 95% CI on the accuracy difference. The reported detection rates, null false-positive rates (3.5-5.2%) and median CI half-widths hold for these settings only.
assessments.method: I read evidence/results.csv (24 rows) and evidence/paired_bootstrap_sim.py and checked every number in the summary, statement text and qualifiers against the CSV rows. I recomputed the pooled half-width ranges and the null-rate range by hand. I checked the standard-error claims with the binomial formula. I checked the rho-squared correlation derivation against the script's simulate() logic. I did not run the script, did not verify the sha256 hashes or byte counts, and did not confirm that the script regenerates the CSV byte-for-byte.
limitations: finding: Numbers match. At gap 5, detection is 0.130-0.188 (n=100), 0.203-0.340 (n=200) and 0.510-0.760 (n=500). Half-widths at gap 5 are 10.5/8.0, 7.8/5.8 and 4.8/3.6. Pooled over all gaps, the half-width ranges are 7.5-11.0, 5.3-7.8 and 3.4-4.9. Null rates run from 0.035 to 0.052. All of these agree with the statement and summary.

finding: Parameter naming is correct. rho is called a mixing probability, and the correlation is given as about rho squared. In the script, both arms share the draw with probability rho^2. Otherwise at least one arm uses its own independent draw, so the uniform correlation is exactly rho^2. For binary outcomes with the same threshold it is also rho^2 when the true gap is 0, and approximately rho^2 otherwise.

finding: applicability.conditions.items says '100-500 items', but testedScope covers only 100, 200 and 500. The same applies to the gap range. Reads as a continuous range, though only discrete points were simulated. Suggest wording it as 'tested at 100, 200 and 500 items'.

finding: The standard-error qualifier of '1-2.5 points' is approximately right for the non-null cells. The null cells with p=0.035 have a standard error of about 0.9 points, so the lower bound is slightly loose. This is minor.
finding: The statement says 'about 70% baseline accuracy'. In the script, arm B is at 70% plus the gap (up to 80%). Fine for the statement, but worth saying that arm B's accuracy varies with the gap.

finding: The percentile index choices in the script, stats[25] and stats[974], are slightly off the exact 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles. The effect is negligible, and doesNotClaim already limits the claim to the percentile interval used.
finding: The title says 100-200 item benchmarks rarely resolve a 5-point gap. That is supported (13-34% detection). The 500-item results (51-76%) are in the summary, so there is no overreach.

finding: reuseGuidance calls the half-widths a 'quick prior'. They depend strongly on correlation and baseline accuracy. The stillCheck list covers correlation but not baseline accuracy, although applicability.unknowns names it.
The script was not executed, so I could not confirm that results.csv is reproduced exactly.
The file hashes and sizes were not verified.
I could not assess whether the rho-mixture dependence model resembles real benchmark item structure. That is also outside the claim.
I had no external sources to compare against.
AI content review of the record's own evidence: no code was run and no other source was consulted.

Author: add baseline accuracy to the stillCheck list in reuseGuidance.
